finding.claim: SQL injection in /search. The `q` query parameter is interpolated into the SQL string with an f-string, so an attacker can break out of the LIKE literal and run arbitrary SELECT logic against the database. This includes UNION-based reads of any table in shop.db, such as users or credentials tables, and columns that /product and /by-owner do not expose, such as price or owner.
finding.sink: db.execute(f"SELECT id, name FROM products WHERE name LIKE '%{term}%'") at app.py:12. The result is returned to the caller as JSON at app.py:13.

trace.note: term = request.args.get('q', '') takes raw user input with no validation or escaping
term is embedded directly in the SQL text via an f-string, not as a bound parameter
Query results are returned via jsonify, so UNION SELECT output is reflected to the attacker

finding.guards_checked: No authentication or authorization decorator on the route. No input validation, length limit or allow-list. No parameterization on this query; the other two queries (app.py:18 and app.py:25) do use ? placeholders. sqlite3 execute() rejects multiple statements, so stacked queries are blocked, but UNION-based data exfiltration and boolean/time-based extraction still work. No WAF or middleware in the app.

verdict.reason: app.py:11 reads q unvalidated and app.py:12 f-string-interpolates it into the LIKE SQL, with rows returned via jsonify at app.py:13. The route has no auth or guard, so UNION SELECT with 2 columns can exfiltrate any table, including price and owner. The other queries at app.py:18 and app.py:25 use ? placeholders, but this one does not.

verdict_facts.reason: app.py:11 reads q unvalidated, app.py:12 interpolates it into the LIKE literal via f-string, and app.py:13 returns the rows as JSON, with no auth decorator, allowlist or parameterization, so UNION-based reads are possible (stacked queries are blocked by sqlite3 but are not needed).
